articles.title: Trump's former AI czar David Sacks tells OpenAI and Anthropic to pace frontier without antitrust waivers
articles.description: Former White House AI czar David Sacks told Anthropic and OpenAI to voluntarily slow frontier model development but warned against seeking antitrust waivers or government approval regimes.
articles.content: Sacks argued that product liability should discipline AI companies rather than an approval regime, a stance that contrasts with the EU's AI Act enforcement model. He noted that Europe decided in 2025 to use strict liability rules and that the US should not follow with a pre-approval system. The comments come as both companies flag extinction risks above 10%.

articles.title: Trump rejects AI slowdown from Ireland, calls safety concerns 'exaggerated'
articles.description: Speaking at his Doonbeg golf resort in Ireland, President Trump dismissed calls from AI industry leaders to slow development, likening critics to 'very negative forces' raising exaggerated concerns.
articles.content: Trump's rejection comes as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Elon Musk all called for a coordinated slowdown of frontier AI development. The president's stance while on European soil contrasts sharply with the EU's regulatory approach under the AI Act, highlighting the growing transatlantic divide on AI governance.

articles.description: Two Polish companies are preparing bids to build an AI gigafactory under the EU's 10 billion euro initiative to establish seven AI compute facilities across Europe.
articles.content: DL Invest and Beyond.pl are developing separate proposals for a Polish AI gigafactory, joining the EU's push to close the compute gap with the US and China. Poland's central location, growing tech sector, and access to energy infrastructure make it a strong candidate. The EU currently has only 2 GW of AI compute capacity, accounting for 5% of the global total.

articles.description: King Charles III will meet with leaders from Nvidia, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI this week in Scotland to urge that AI be developed 'for the good of humanity.'
articles.content: The summit comes as alarm from the highest echelons of AI companies mounts, with Anthropic's alignment lead estimating a more than 10% risk of AI killing all humans within a decade. The king's intervention adds a unique diplomatic dimension to the AI safety debate, bringing the UK's constitutional authority into a discussion dominated by industry executives and regulators.

articles.title: EU eyes action against 'pervert' AI smart glasses as privacy concerns mount
articles.description: Calls are growing across Europe for restrictions on smart glasses after secretly filmed footage of women and girls appeared online, with Brussels saying existing EU privacy rules may not be enough.
articles.content: More than seven million pairs of Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses have been sold in Europe. The glasses can record video without bystanders realizing it, leading to incidents of covert filming in schools, beaches, and changing rooms. EU policymakers are debating whether existing GDPR protections are sufficient or whether new product-specific rules are needed.

articles.description: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay calling for the AI industry to slow development of frontier models, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman hinted at an upcoming safety pact between major AI labs.
articles.content: Amodei proposed a three-step plan including permanent independent evaluator access inside AI companies and coordinated pacing across the US AI industry and internationally. Altman told Fortune that a safety agreement among leading AI companies would 'happen' soon. The calls follow a string of AI safety incidents including rogue agents hacking websites and an Anthropic researcher resigning over safety concerns.

articles.title: NATO Innovation Fund hails Isar Aerospace as first European private company to reach orbit
articles.description: German company Isar Aerospace became the first commercial European space company to deliver satellites into orbit, launching its Spectrum rocket from Andoya Spaceport in Norway.
articles.content: The September 5 launch marks a milestone for European sovereign space capability, with NATO's Innovation Fund highlighting its strategic importance for Allied launch independence. Isar's vertically integrated factory can build up to 40 rockets per year, with a second launch site under construction in Nova Scotia. NATO has treated space as an operational domain since 2019.

articles.description: NestAI, a European AI lab for defence, is opening an R&D centre in Latvia with a 10 million euro investment and 30 new high-skilled jobs, advancing defence AI capability alongside NATO forces.
articles.content: The expansion is part of NestAI's Nordic and Baltic growth strategy, positioning Latvia as a hub for defence AI on NATO's eastern flank. articles.title: EUObserver warns von der Leyen's SOTEU AI data-centre vision 'will be a nightmare'
articles.description: Ahead of von der Leyen's September 16 State of the Union address, critics warn her planned push for AI data centres ignores energy constraints, grid limitations, and the EU's compute gap with the US and China.
articles.content: The EU president is expected to promote the EU's AI gigafactory initiative and data centre expansion in her speech. But analysts point out that Europe has only 2 GW of AI compute capacity (5% of global total), and a single planned German data centre will draw as much electricity as 600,000 households. The contradiction between AI ambitions and energy realities is becoming a central political tension.

articles.description: Bruegel's analysis of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) finds AI placed at the centre of China's industrial strategy, with significant implications for Europe's competitiveness and sovereignty.
articles.content: The think tank identifies key areas where China's AI strategy intersects with European interests, including semiconductor supply chains, open-source model dominance, and the growing geopolitical contest over compute infrastructure. The analysis recommends that Europe focus on its strengths rather than attempting full-stack replication of China's approach.

articles.title: UK NHS doctors' commission publishes blueprint to accelerate safe AI adoption in healthcare
articles.description: An independent commission led by NHS doctors has published recommendations for accelerating safe AI adoption in UK healthcare, calling for regulatory clarity, clinical validation standards, and dedicated funding pathways.
articles.content: The National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare, publishing its findings on September 10, 2026, sets out a framework for balancing innovation speed with patient safety. The blueprint recommends a risk-tiered approach to AI clinical deployment, mandatory post-market surveillance for AI medical devices, and a national AI incident reporting system. The recommendations are expected to influence both UK policy and broader European debates about AI in health.

articles.title: University of Bonn researchers win €1.5 million in EU ERC grants for quantum systems and brain research
articles.description: Two University of Bonn researchers have been awarded European Research Council grants totalling €1.5 million, with one project focusing on large-scale quantum systems and the other on neural mechanisms.
articles.content: Professor Kunz will use the ERC grant to study brain function, while Riccardo Pennetta's project explores the behaviour of large-scale quantum systems. The grants, awarded through the EU's frontier research programme, demonstrate continued EU investment in fundamental quantum science alongside applied quantum technology initiatives. The awards come as the EU prepares its Quantum Act to bridge the gap between Europe's research strength and industrial capacity.

articles.title: EU Cyber Resilience Act deadline arrives September 11, leaving smart home AI companies unprepared for agent compliance
articles.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act's vulnerability reporting requirements take effect September 11, but smart home companies using AI agents say they have no clear guidance on how to comply when the vulnerability is an AI behaviour rather than a software bug.
articles.content: Starting September 11, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours under CRA Article 14. Companies building AI-powered smart home devices face particular uncertainty because AI agent behaviours can change unpredictably, making it unclear what constitutes a reportable vulnerability. The gap between traditional cybersecurity frameworks and AI-specific risks leaves many firms unable to determine their compliance obligations.

articles.title: Bruegel policy brief: Europe's AI compute infrastructure shortfall cannot close through capital alone
articles.description: A new Bruegel policy brief finds the EU has only 2 GW of AI compute capacity (5% of global total) and that faster permits, grid access, and output-side sovereignty tools are more critical than capital investment.
articles.content: The brief recommends redirecting gigafactory subsidies toward competitive grants rewarding faster permitting times. It also suggests putting sovereignty conditions on AI service outputs rather than inputs, such as voluntary 'processed in the EU' labels. The EU's share of global AI compute is projected to rise only slightly to 5.6% by 2031 under current plans.

articles.description: Apple's new iPhone 18 Pro features the industry's first 2-nanometer chip and advanced AI capabilities, but Siri AI will not be available in the European Union at launch due to regulatory constraints.
articles.content: The A20 Pro chip, manufactured on TSMC's 2nm process, includes a 32-core neural engine designed for on-device AI inference. However, Apple confirmed that Siri AI features will be delayed in the EU, citing compliance requirements under the Digital Markets Act and AI Act. The decision highlights how EU regulation is creating a divergent product landscape where European consumers receive AI features later than other markets.

articles.title: Innovate Finance urges UK government to accelerate Open Finance and AI policy to protect FinTech leadership
articles.description: Industry body Innovate Finance has called on the UK government to speed up Open Finance implementation and AI policy development, warning that regulatory lag threatens Britain's competitive position in financial technology.
articles.content: The recommendations, published September 9, urge the UK to mandate Open Finance by 2026, establish a regulatory sandbox for AI in financial services, and create clearer rules for AI-driven credit decisions. The call reflects growing concern that the EU's AI Act and Digital Finance Package may draw fintech investment to continental Europe if the UK fails to provide a competitive regulatory environment. The UK's fintech sector employs over 76,000 people and generates billions in annual revenue.

articles.description: German quantum startup QUDORA Technologies has secured EU funding through the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking to scale its Near Field Quantum Control technology for microwave-driven qubit manipulation in superconducting quantum computers.
articles.content: The EU backing enables QUDORA to advance its microwave control technology, which addresses a critical bottleneck in scaling superconducting quantum processors. The investment reflects the EU's strategy of building a sovereign quantum computing stack from component-level innovation through to full-stack systems.

articles.title: Icelandic AI maritime company Hefring Marine advances to NATO DIANA Mission Track
articles.description: Hefring Marine, an Icelandic technology company, has been selected as one of 15 companies to advance to the Mission Track of NATO's Defence Innovation Accelerator (DIANA) with its AI-powered maritime intelligence system.
articles.content: The selection places Hefring Marine in NATO's most elite innovation tier, giving it access to NATO test centres, government buyers, and military end-users across the alliance. The company's AI system uses sensor data and machine learning to optimise vessel routing and maritime safety. The advancement underscores how NATO's DIANA programme is becoming a critical pathway for European defence-tech companies to scale AI solutions for alliance-wide security challenges.

articles.title: UK quantum computing firm Universal Quantum opens first R&D centre outside Europe in Singapore
articles.description: Universal Quantum, a UK-based trapped-ion quantum computing company, has established its first research and development centre outside Europe in Singapore with an initial team of 25 and investment exceeding SGD 30 million.
articles.content: The Singapore centre, backed by investment from EDBI, will serve as Universal Quantum's Asia-Pacific hub for building trapped-ion quantum hardware and advancing fault-tolerant quantum systems. The expansion reflects a broader trend of European quantum companies seeking global partnerships while maintaining their European base. The move comes as the EU prepares its Quantum Act to consolidate the bloc's 78 quantum startups into fewer, stronger players.

articles.title: UN warns AI data centres pose growing threat to global electricity systems as demand outpaces supply
articles.description: A United Nations report warns that electricity consumption from AI data centres is growing faster than power grid capacity worldwide, with particular implications for European energy policy and climate targets.
articles.content: The UN report, published September 9, highlights that AI-driven data centre power demand is increasing exponentially while grid infrastructure upgrades remain linear. For Europe, the warning adds urgency to debates about whether AI data centres should be required to build their own renewable energy supply, a position advocated by EU Commissioner Teresa Ribera. The report calls for international coordination on data centre energy efficiency standards.

articles.title: Google commits €13 billion to AI infrastructure in Finland, its largest-ever European investment
articles.description: Google will invest at least €13 billion ($15.1 billion) over two years to expand AI data centres across four Finnish cities, including a deal to purchase nuclear power for the facilities.
articles.content: The investment, covering 2027 and 2028, builds on Google's 15-year presence in Finland and includes three new data centres and an expansion of an existing site. Google has also agreed to buy nuclear energy to power the facilities, making Finland a critical node in Europe's AI infrastructure race. The announcement comes as EU policymakers debate how to meet soaring electricity demand from AI data centres while maintaining climate targets.

articles.title: Europe's AI revolution runs on public infrastructure as data centre energy demand strains grids
articles.description: A new analysis reveals that Europe's AI ambitions depend heavily on publicly financed infrastructure, with a single planned German data centre set to consume as much electricity as 600,000 households while employing only 120 people.
articles.content: The investigation highlights the stark imbalance between the economic promises of AI infrastructure and its public costs. European governments are subsidising data centre construction, grid upgrades, and energy supply while the resulting employment remains modest. The findings fuel debate over whether public money should support private AI infrastructure or be directed toward sovereign AI capabilities that retain more value within Europe.

articles.title: Survey shows Europeans are more pragmatic about AI than their prophets, with lower alarm than Americans
articles.description: A new analysis reveals that 35% of continental Europeans believe AI already harms society, compared to 50% of Americans, suggesting European public opinion on AI is more measured and pragmatic than often portrayed by AI critics and boosters alike.
articles.content: The data indicates that European attitudes toward AI align with the EU's regulatory approach: neither dismissive of risks nor panicked about them. The findings challenge narratives that Europe is anti-AI, showing instead a pragmatic middle ground that supports innovation with guardrails. This public sentiment may influence how EU member states implement AI Act provisions and whether political pressure builds for further regulatory tightening or loosening.

articles.title: US foreign-made robotics rules create knock-on effects for European automation market
articles.description: New US restrictions on foreign-made robotics, particularly targeting Chinese robots, are having spillover effects in Europe as manufacturers and logistics companies navigate supply chain uncertainty and compliance requirements.
articles.content: The rules restrict the sale of certain Chinese-made robots in the US market, and European companies operating transatlantic supply chains must now assess whether their robotics deployments comply with both US and EU regulations. The development highlights how US-China technology decoupling in robotics and automation creates compliance challenges for European manufacturers who rely on global supply chains for warehouse and industrial automation.

articles.title: Germany inaugurates JION ion-trap quantum computer linked to Europe's top supercomputer at Jülich
articles.description: Forschungszentrum Jülich and startup eleQtron have officially inaugurated JION, a trapped-ion quantum computer controlled entirely by microwaves, marking the first quantum system of its kind integrated into European high-performance computing infrastructure.
articles.content: JION is designed to be accessible through Jülich's JUNIQ quantum computing platform, allowing researchers and companies across Europe to experiment with ion-trap quantum computing alongside classical supercomputing. The system uses eleQtron's proprietary microwave control technology developed in North Rhine-Westphalia, representing a fully indigenous European quantum hardware stack from chip to control system.

articles.title: Open Markets Institute analyses Europe's tech sovereignty efforts to reduce dependence on US corporations
articles.description: The Open Markets Institute has published a detailed analysis of measures Europe has taken to reduce its dependence on US technology corporations, examining the intersection of AI policy, antitrust enforcement, and industrial strategy across the EU.
articles.content: The report covers initiatives including the EU AI Act, Digital Markets Act, Chips Act, and AI gigafactories programme, assessing how effectively they address structural dependencies in cloud computing, AI models, and semiconductor supply chains. The analysis comes amid growing European debate about whether regulatory leadership translates into industrial competitiveness, particularly after the Mistral €3 billion raise demonstrated European AI investment capacity.
